Pip the squirrel was quite certain that no creature in the whole garden was half so quick as he. He had just finished his morning's exercise, which was to race from the top of the old stone wall to the tip of the highest sunflower and back again, three times without stopping. "Did you see me?" he chattered to Old Man Thistlewick, the ancient rabbit who was nibbling placidly on a clover patch. "I believe I was faster than the wind itself today!"

Old Man Thistlewick chewed thoughtfully for a moment. "You were indeed moving in a great hurry, Pip," he agreed. "But what is the good of such speed when there is no fox behind you?"

"It is not about a fox!" Pip exclaimed, flicking his tail. "It is about being the best! The oak tree is dropping its acorns now. I shall have my winter pantry full before anyone else has even gathered a dozen. I will simply be too fast for them!"

"That is one way to do it," Thistlewick said slowly. "But one acorn at a time is a great many trips, no matter how fast your legs are."

"My legs are the fastest!" Pip declared. And with a whisk of his tail, he was gone, a little brown blur streaking across the lawn toward the mighty oak.

He scrambled up the trunk, seized the first acorn he saw, and scurried back to the hollow in the maple tree that he called home. He dropped the acorn inside with a satisfying clatter. Then he was off again. Back and forth he went, his little heart pounding with effort and pride.

A noisy blue jay named Jasper, who was watching from a branch, began to laugh. "What a busy squirrel!" he squawked. "Look at him go! One nut, then another! At this rate, you might be finished by next spring!"

Pip felt his ears grow warm. He ignored the jay and tried to go even faster. But in his haste, he fumbled his next acorn. It bounced off a root and rolled into a puddle. "Oh dear!" he cried, stopping for a moment. His paws were muddy and his breath was coming in short, sharp gasps. He looked at his little hoard. There were only seven acorns. And he was already quite tired.

With his tail drooping, he trotted slowly back to the clover patch, where Old Man Thistlewick was still enjoying his breakfast. "It is harder work than I thought," Pip admitted in a small voice. "And Jasper the jay made fun of me."

Thistlewick nodded. "Jasper is a noisy fellow," he said. "But perhaps he is not entirely wrong. Come with me. I will show you something."

He led Pip not to the oak tree, but to a place behind the woodpile where a large, curved piece of bark lay on the ground. "What is this for?" Pip asked.

"This is my wagon," the old rabbit announced. "Now, watch." Thistlewick went to the oak tree and began to nudge acorns with his nose. Instead of carrying them one by one, he rolled them all to the piece of bark. Soon, there was a great pile of more than twenty acorns sitting on it. Then, Thistlewick got behind the bark and began to push it slowly and steadily across the lawn. It was not fast, but it was very effective.

"Goodness!" Pip cried. "You have gathered more in one trip than I did in seven! And you are not even out of breath."

"Speed is a fine thing, Pip," Old Man Thistlewick said kindly as he reached the maple tree. "But sometimes, a clever plan is better than quick feet. Would you care for some help with your pantry?"

Pip looked at the pile of acorns, then at his empty paws, and then at the wise old rabbit. "Yes, please!" he said. "I think I would like to learn how to use a wagon."

After the pine grove, the path widened and led into an open meadow. The ground was soft and spongy, like a great wet carpet. Here and there, large puddles had formed, some of them as big as a wagon.

"We'll have to go around the big ones," Farmer Green said. "No telling how deep they are."

Twinkleheels ignored her. He kept his eyes on Johnnie and his ears tuned for Farmer Green's voice.

This only made Bessie more determined. "My old owner, Mr. Higgins, he always said I was the bravest horse in the rain. I'm not afraid of mud."

To prove her point, instead of following the others on the wide detour around the next puddle, Bessie decided to walk right through the middle of a smaller one. It was a shallow, muddy pool, and she splashed through it with her head held high.

"See?" she called out, as if she had performed a great feat. "It's just water."

Farmer Green shook his head but said nothing.

They continued on. The orchard was now in sight, just across one last, wide, boggy stretch of field. This was the worst part. The water from the melting snows had collected here, turning the whole area into a soupy morass of mud and grass. There seemed to be no clear path.

"I think we should stick to the very edge," Farmer Green said, pointing to where the field met a line of rocks. "It looks a little higher there."

But Bessie had another idea. She had been embarrassed, and she wanted to redeem herself. She saw a line of grassy humps that seemed to make a sort of path right through the middle of the bog. It looked like a shortcut. If she could get across first, she could prove that she was the smarter, braver horse.

"That way is for cowards!" she suddenly announced. "A real horse makes its own path!"

And before Silas could grab her lead rope securely, she gave a great tug, pulled free, and trotted briskly towards the line of grassy humps.

"Bessie! Come back here!" Silas yelled.

Farmer Green looked at the terrified horse, then at the sled, then at Twinkleheels. He took his hat off and scratched his head.

"Well, Johnnie," he said quietly. "It seems our job just got a bit more complicated."

Johnnie Green spoke a quiet word to the oxen. "Get up, Bright. Get up, Broad."

Then, slowly, surely, she began to move. Bright and Broad took another step, and then another. The mud made a loud sucking sound as it released its grip. With a great squelch, Bessie was pulled free from the bog and onto firmer ground. She stood there, dripping with mud and trembling from head to foot, but she was safe.
After that, it was the wagon's turn. The oxen pulled it out just as easily.
Mr. Pringle could not thank Farmer Green enough. "I don't know what I would have done," he said again and again. "You and your boys and your wonderful animals have saved the day."
"Glad we could help," Farmer Green said simply.

It was the slow, steady strength of Bright and Broad that had done the real work. He looked at the two huge, patient creatures, chewing their cuds as if nothing at all had happened, and he felt a new kind of respect for them. They were not fast, and they were not flashy, but when it came to a hard job, they were the ones you needed.

XIX WISDOM IN THE STALL

It was late in the afternoon when Twinkleheels was finally led back to his own stall, right next to old Ebenezer. He was bursting with the news of the day's adventure. "Ebenezer! You won't believe what happened!" he began, even before Johnnie had finished unbuckling his halter.
"Let me guess," the old horse said, opening one sleepy eye. "You used your new shoes to race a rabbit and you won."
"No! Much better than that!" Twinkleheels exclaimed. And he told Ebenezer the whole story. He told about the prideful mare Bessie, and her boasting, and how she had ignored Farmer Green's advice. He told of her mad dash across the bog, and the terrible, sinking moment when the ground gave way. He described the rescue in great detail, making sure to mention the important role of Bright and Broad.
Ebenezer listened patiently, nodding his head now and then. When Twinkleheels had finished, the old horse was quiet for a long time.
"Well," he said at last. "It sounds as if that mare learned what a heavy burden pride can be."
"She certainly did!" Twinkleheels agreed. "She was stuck fast! She looked very silly."
"Did she?" Ebenezer asked quietly. "Or did she look frightened? And cold? And humbled?"
Twinkleheels thought for a moment. "Well, yes," he admitted. "She looked all of those things, too."
"Pride is a tricky thing," Ebenezer went on, his voice soft and thoughtful. "It can make you feel tall and strong, like your new shoes made you feel. But it can also make you blind to danger. It can make you think your own path is better than the well-trodden one. And more often than not, it leads straight into a bog." He shifted his weight from one foot to another. "I suspect that poor mare won't be taking any more shortcuts for a good long while."

"I suppose," Twinklehes said slowly, "that it is better to be safe than to be fast."
"It is better to be wise than to be proud," Ebenezer corrected him gently. "And wisdom, my young friend, is usually found on the path that has been traveled by many feet before you."

He thought about the strong, silent oxen, and the calm, capable Farmer Green, and the foolish, humbled Bessie. It had been a very big day, full of excitement and important lessons. And as he drifted off to sleep, Twinkleheels decided that while new shoes were very fine things indeed, a wise friend in the next stall was worth even more.

Her owner stood on the solid edge of the bog, wringing his hands and shouting uselessly.

Ebenezer opened an eye. "That looks like Farmer Green's cousin, Mr. Davis," he said. "And that must be his new saddle horse. I've heard he's very proud of him."

Mr. Davis, a man with a booming voice and a fancy coat, greeted Farmer Green. "Just thought I'd stop by on my way to town," he declared. "Wanted to show you my new gelding. Isn't he a beauty? Name's Gallant. Fast as the wind, he is."

Farmer Green looked the horse over with a practiced eye. "He's a fine looking animal, to be sure," he admitted.

"Fine looking and fine going!" Mr. Davis boasted. "He can cover ten miles before one of your plow horses has finished his breakfast."

Johnnie led Twinkleheels to his stall, and a moment later, Mr. Davis led the magnificent Gallant into the barn. He put him in the stall next to Twinkleheels, the one Bessie had occupied.

Gallant looked around the barn with a disdainful air. He eyed Ebenezer's thick legs and Broad's wide back in the adjoining cattle stalls. Then his gaze fell upon Twinkleheels.

Twinkleheels felt his ears get hot. "I am not a pasture pony," he said, trying to make his voice sound dignified. "I have a job. I pull a cart for Johnnie Green."

"A cart!" Gallant snorted, a sound that was surprisingly rude for such a handsome horse. "How thrilling. I, on the other hand, am a gentleman's saddle horse. I do not 'pull' things. I carry my master with speed and grace. I have won three silver cups in racing exhibitions."

Ebenezer, who had been listening quietly, shifted his weight. "Those 'plodding beasts'," he said, his voice a low rumble, "pulled a very proud mare out of the bog a few days ago. A mare who thought she was faster than good sense."

Gallant tossed his head. "A clumsy animal, no doubt. A truly fine horse, a horse with breeding and speed like myself, would never find himself in such a predicament. We are too clever for that."

Perhaps, he thought, being fast and flashy was better after all.

"Now then," said Farmer Green to the smith. "This little fellow is here for his first set of shoes. Be gentle with him, Sam. He's never had it done before."

The blacksmith, whose name was Sam, nodded and smiled a kindly smile that made his face wrinkle around his eyes. "Don't you worry, Farmer Green," he said, his voice a deep, friendly rumble. "I'll treat him like he was my own. Now, little one, let's have a look at those feet."

Twinkleheels remembered what Ebenezer had told him. He stood as still as he could while Sam came near. The blacksmith ran a knowing hand down Twinkleheels' leg and then said, "Up now." He tapped the back of the pony's leg, and almost without thinking, Twinkleheels lifted his foot.

"There's a good fellow!" Sam said. He rested the pony's hoof on his leather apron and began to work. He cleaned it out with a special tool, and then he trimmed the edge of the hoof with a sharp knife. Twinkleheels flinched, but it didn't hurt at all. It felt more like having his fingernails cut, if a pony had fingernails.

Then came the shoe. Sam brought it from the forge, where he had shaped it. It was cool now. He held it against Twinkleheels' hoof to check the size. "A perfect fit," he declared.

Then he took some long, thin nails. This was the part Twinkleheels had dreaded. He held his breath. Sam placed the nail against the hoof and with a few quick, sharp taps of his hammer, he drove it in. Twinkleheels braced himself for a terrible pain, but he felt nothing at all! He felt only the slight jar of the hammer blows. The blacksmith drove in several more nails and then twisted off their sharp ends.

He did the same with the other three feet. And with each one, Twinkleheels grew more confident and less afraid. He found the whole process quite interesting. When the last shoe was on, Sam patted him on the neck. "There you are, all done," he said. "You're a brave little pony. You stood better than many a full-grown horse I've shod."

Twinkleheels felt like bursting with pride. He looked down at his new iron shoes. They felt strange and a little heavy, but they made a most satisfactory clinking sound on the hard floor of the smithy.

Johnnie Green came and untied him. "You were wonderful, Twinkleheels!" he said, stroking his nose.

Twinkleheels could hardly wait to try out his new shoes. He followed Johnnie out of the shop, lifting his feet high and listening to the fine new sound they made on the ground. Ebenezer, who had been shod while Twinkleheels was watching, followed them out.

"How do they feel?" the old horse asked.

"They feel grand!" Twinkleheels exclaimed. "I feel as if I could race the wind itself!" He gave a little skip and kick, just to hear the shoes clatter.

"Don't let them go to your head," Ebenezer advised, though there was a kindly twinkle in his eye. "Shoes are for work, not for showing off. Remember that."

But Twinkleheels was almost too excited to listen. He felt stronger, faster, and more important than he ever had before.

XVII A BOASTFUL GUEST

The next morning, the barn was filled with a new sound. It was the sound of Gallant, the handsome bay horse, pacing restlessly in his stall. He would walk three steps to the front, toss his head, and then walk three steps to the back. His specially weighted shoes made a crisp, important tapping on the wooden floor.

"I cannot bear to be idle," he announced to the barn at large. "On a fine morning like this, my master and I would usually be flying across the fields, the dew scattering before my hooves. This standing about is for cattle, not for a horse of my quality." He cast a scornful glance towards Bright and Broad, who were placidly chewing their breakfast.

Twinkleheels listened from his stall. Part of him felt annoyed at Gallant's rudeness. But another part of him was still quite dazzled. Gallant was so sure of himself; he seemed to come from another world, a world of speed and silver cups. Compared to that, a life of pulling a cart seemed very plain indeed.

When Johnnie Green came to lead him to the watering trough, Twinkleheels tried to imitate Gallant. He held his head very high and tried to make his new shoes strike the ground with the same crisp authority.

Old Ebenezer, in the stall next to him, watched with quiet amusement. "You seem to have a new way of walking this morning, Twinkleheels," he remarked as the pony passed.

"One must keep up appearances," Twinkleheels said, trying to sound as worldly as Gallant. "A horse is judged by his bearing."

Ebenezer just blinked his old eyes slowly. "A horse is judged by his deeds, little one," he said. "Bearing won't pull a plow or get you out of a mud hole."

Twinkleheels felt his ears grow a little warm, but he pretended not to hear. He took a long drink at the trough and then strutted back to the barn, pleased with the clatter of his own hooves.

Just then, Farmer Green came into the barn, looking troubled. "Johnnie," he said, "that big old oak at the edge of the lower pasture finally came down in the wind last night. It's fallen right across the path, and it's blocking the way for the cows."

"That's a big tree, Father," Johnnie said.

"It is," Farmer Green agreed. "And the ground is soft from the thaw. It's a mucky mess down there. We'll have to saw it into logs and drag them out of the way. I'll need some real strength for this job."

From his stall, Gallant let out a neigh that sounded like a laugh. "Strength?" he said, loud enough for the humans to hear, though of course they did not understand his words. "Why bother with strength when you can have speed and grace? I could leap such a log without a second thought! A true gentleman's horse is an athlete, not a lumbering brute."

Twinkleheels glanced at Ebenezer, expecting him to say something. But the old horse was silent, his gaze fixed on Farmer Green.

"I'll get the harness for Bright and Broad," Farmer Green said, making up his mind. "There's no horse on this farm that could budge that timber, not on that slippery ground. This is a job for oxen."

"Can I bring Twinkleheels?" Johnnie asked. "He can carry the water jug and the extra chain."

"A good idea," said his father. "We'll lead Gallant along, too. His owner said he needed some exercise, and he'll be safer with us than left alone in the barn."

A short while later, the strange procession set off. Bright and Broad walked first, their heavy yokes creaking, their pace slow and deliberate. Farmer Green walked beside them. Johnnie followed, leading Twinkleheels, who had a small coil of rope on his back. Behind them all, a stable hand from the next farm, who had come to help, led the elegant Gallant.

Gallant did not like the arrangement one bit. He danced and sidled, pulling at his lead rope. "This is humiliating!" he muttered to Twinkleheels. "Forced to walk behind these plodding beasts. The shame of it! And look at you, turned into a pack mule. Is this what you call having a job?"

Twinkleheels felt a sting of resentment. "I'm helping," he said defensively.

"You're carrying a rope," Gallant sneered. "I carry champions to victory. There is a difference."

They soon reached the lower pasture. The scene was just as Farmer Green had described. A huge oak tree lay across the path. Its trunk was as thick as a barrel, and its roots had torn a great wound in the earth. The ground all around was a churned-up sea of mud, gleaming wetly in the morning sun.

Bright and Broad stood patiently, their breath misting in the cool air, while Farmer Green surveyed the problem.

"Hmph," Gallant snorted. "All this fuss for a fallen branch. Why, I could clear that in a single bound. You are all wasting the morning."

Farmer Green began to attach a heavy chain to the thickest part of the log. The work was slow and difficult in the thick mud.

"Watch this, little pony," Gallant whispered to Twinkleheels. His eyes were gleaming with a wild, reckless light. "I will show these farm creatures what a real horse can do. They plod and pull; I fly!"

Before the stable hand could stop him, Gallant gathered himself. He took a few quick, powerful strides backward, finding what looked like a patch of firmer ground. His muscles bunched beneath his sleek coat.

"Don't do it!" Twinkleheels wanted to cry out, but the words stuck in his throat. He remembered Bessie the mare, and the bog.

With a great surge of power, Gallant launched himself forward. He was a magnificent sight, soaring through the air, his legs tucked neatly beneath him. For a moment, it looked as if he would make it. He cleared the heavy trunk of the oak with inches to spare.

But he had not accounted for the landing.

His sharp hooves did not find the solid earth he expected. They plunged into the softest, deepest part of the mud on the other side of the log. There was a sickening, sucking sound. Gallant landed with a jolt that shook his whole body. He tried to spring forward, to find his footing, but his legs only sank deeper. The mud was like a thick, greedy glue. It clung to his slender legs, pulling him down.

He panicked. He let out a terrified squeal and began to struggle wildly, thrashing and lunging. But his frantic movements only made his plight worse. With every desperate heave, he sank deeper and deeper, until the mud was nearly up to his belly.

XVIII A LESSON IN CHAINS

Gallant stood trembling, his beautiful coat spattered with black mud. The proud, arrogant horse was gone. In his place was a frightened animal, trapped and helpless. He had stopped struggling and now stood with his head hanging low, his breath coming in ragged gasps.

Farmer Green walked slowly to the edge of the mud pit and shook his head. He looked not angry, but weary. "Pride is a poor tool for this kind of work," he said quietly to Johnnie. "And a poor guide, too. Speed is no good without sense."

He turned his attention back to the problem at hand. "All right," he said, his voice firm and practical once more. "First, we get the horse out. Then, we get the log out."

He unhitched the heavy chain from the oak tree. He spoke in a low, calm voice to Bright and Broad, who had watched the entire affair with their great, placid eyes. They did not seem surprised at all. They simply stood and waited, as they always did.

Farmer Green and the stable hand waded carefully into the mud, carrying the chain. They worked it under Gallant's belly, making a sort of sling. It was dirty, difficult work. Gallant flinched when the cold metal touched him, but he was too exhausted and defeated to protest.

"Easy now, boy," Farmer Green said, patting the horse's muddy neck.

He attached the ends of the chain to the oxen's yoke. "Now, Johnnie," he said. "You stand by that horse's head. Talk to him. Keep him calm."

Johnnie waded in as close as he dared and began to stroke Gallant's nose, speaking to him in the same soft tones he used with Twinkleheels. "It's all right," he murmured. "They'll get you out. Just be still."

From the edge of the path, Twinkleheels watched, his heart thumping. He had never seen such a thing.

"Now, Bright! Now, Broad! Heave!" Farmer Green called out.

There was no sudden jerk. There was no grand display of effort. The two great oxen simply leaned forward into their yoke. The muscles in their broad backs swelled. The chain groaned and tightened, lifting out of the mud. For a moment, nothing seemed to happen. Gallant was held fast.

"Heave!" Farmer Green called again.

Bright and Broad lowered their heads and pushed. They dug their big, cloven hooves into the ground, finding traction where Gallant's slim ones had found none. Slowly, inch by inch, with a great sucking, slurping sound, Gallant was dragged forward. The oxen did not hurry. Their power was a slow, immense, irresistible tide. They pulled the handsome horse right out of the mud pit and onto the firmer ground of the path.

As soon as he was free, Gallant staggered and almost fell. He was covered from his belly to his hooves in thick, stinking mud. His sleek coat was ruined. His pride was gone. He stood with his head down, shivering, and did not look at anyone.

Farmer Green quietly unhooked the chain from him and led the oxen back to the fallen oak. Without a word, he and the stable hand reattached the chain to the log.

"All right, boys," Farmer Green said. "Let's finish the job."

Once more, he called, "Heave!"

And once more, the oxen leaned into their work. The log was tremendously heavy. At first, it did not budge. But Bright and Broad did not falter. They kept the pressure on, a steady, unyielding force. A small root snapped with a sound like a pistol shot. The log scraped and shuddered. Then, slowly, powerfully, it began to move. The oxen dragged the great timber clear across the muddy path and left it resting on the grass, as easily as if it had been a small branch.

Twinkleheels watched the whole thing in silent awe. He had seen Gallant, with all his speed and grace, leap into disaster. And now he had seen Bright and Broad, with their slow, plodding steps, perform a feat of impossible strength. He looked at Gallant, shivering and mud-caked, and then at the two calm oxen, who were already trying to nibble at a patch of clover.

He suddenly felt very foolish for having been so impressed with Gallant's boasts. He looked at his own small body and his own new shoes. He knew he could not jump like Gallant, nor pull like Bright and Broad. But he could carry a water jug. He could pull Johnnie's cart. He was dependable. And for the first time, he understood what Ebenezer had meant. Being dependable was its own kind of strength.

The trip back to the barn was very quiet. Gallant walked with his head low, and he did not prance or pull at his rope. He just squelched.

Later that afternoon, a smart-looking buggy pulled into the farmyard. It was Mr. Davis, come to collect his horse. When he saw the state of Gallant, his jaw dropped.

"What on earth happened?" he cried.

Farmer Green explained what had occurred, simply and without blame. "He's got a bit of spirit, that one," he finished. "But the ground down there is no place for a high-stepper."

Mr. Davis looked from his humbled, muddy horse to the two clean, powerful oxen munching hay in their stalls. He looked very embarrassed. "I... I see," he stammered. "I do apologize, Farmer Green. He can be a bit... proud."

They spent a long time washing Gallant down. When he was finally led away, he looked cleaner, but he did not look proud. He did not even glance at Twinkleheels as he left.

That evening, as the barn settled into the quiet of dusk, Twinkleheels shifted in his stall. The comforting smell of hay and old wood filled the air.

"Ebenezer?" he said softly.

"I am here, little one," the old horse's voice rumbled from the next stall.

"I think I was very silly today," Twinkleheels confessed. "I wanted to be like Gallant. I thought being fast and flashy was the most important thing."

Ebenezer was silent for a long moment. Then he said, "It is easy to be dazzled by a shiny coat and a quick pace. Many are. But a shiny coat will not keep you warm in a storm, and a quick pace will not pull you from the mud."

"Bright and Broad pulled him out," Twinkleheels said, picturing it again. "They are so slow, but they are so strong."

"They are," Ebenezer agreed. "They have their work, and they do it well. Gallant has his work, which is to run fast on a smooth track. He is very good at that, I am sure. But he was in the wrong place today. He did not understand the job. The most important thing for any horse, or any ox, is to understand your own work, and to do it faithfully. Speed has its place, little one. But strength and good sense will carry you farther in the end."

Twinkleheels thought about this. He thought about pulling his little cart for Johnnie, and carrying the water jug, and standing still to be shod. They were not glorious tasks, like winning silver cups. But they were his tasks. And he was good at them.

"I think," Twinkleheels said at last, a new contentment settling over him like a warm blanket, "I think I like being a dependable pony."

"And that," rumbled old Ebenezer, "is a very fine thing to be."
